16 of 64 matches were played under high environmental stress; under high stress, high-intensity running was lower (24.8 vs 26.9 m/min) and sprints were ~10% fewer, while total distance and playing time were preserved.
Only two of the 64 matches were played at air temperatures above 30 °C.

15 time-loss illnesses were recorded (1.1 per 1000 competition days); 12 (80%) were respiratory infections.
30 of 32 teams used central medical services at least once; imaging was the most requested service; 17 teams requested additional equipment or clinical assistance.
Host cities spanned ~4300 km east-west; extreme heat was expected in 14 of 16 host cities (historical maximum WBGT 21-35 °C).
FIFA introduced mandatory 3-minute hydration breaks at the 22nd minute of each half in every match, regardless of conditions.

41 medical-attention illnesses (4.2/1000 player-days) and 8 time-loss illnesses (0.8/1000 player-days); respiratory illness was most frequent.
Incidence of mental-health problems requiring attention was low (0.2 per 1000 player-days).
Injury stoppages were more frequent in women's matches (81.2 vs 56.8 per 1000 match-hours), but women were less often substituted after an incident (15.3% vs 27.3%).
Session RPE for comparable running volumes was higher in the luteal phase, and fatigue 48 h post-match was greater in luteal than follicular phase.
Injury rates were higher in the late luteal phase (IIRR 2.30 vs menstruation), particularly for muscle and non-contact injuries.
Most-used monitoring tools were subjective wellness, heart rate, minutes played and daily medical screening; barriers were time, schedule uncertainty and variable club recommendations.
Of 196 responding players, 15% had no permanent medical staff at their domestic club; two-thirds used FIFA 11+.
When assessing suspected concussion, 55% of medical staff reported feeling pressured by players and 47% by coaching staff.

Core temperature is higher in the luteal than follicular phase at rest and after exercise in the heat.

Neuromuscular training (>=10 min, twice weekly) reduced ACL injuries by 61% (high certainty) and ankle sprains by 39%.

Brazil's largest dengue epidemic: ~6 million probable cases and ~4000 confirmed deaths by June 2024; Brazil was first to include the tetravalent (TAK-003) vaccine in its public system.
Oropouche virus re-emerged in Brazil in 2023-2024.

Yellow fever vaccination is recommended for travellers to most host states (including Distrito Federal, Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul) but not Pernambuco or Ceara; arboviral outbreaks peak in the November-May rainy season.
FIFA's historical policy makes cooling breaks mandatory above WBGT 32 °C; FIFPRO recommends cooling breaks at WBGT 28-32 °C and rescheduling above 32 °C.

74 of 100 computational biology papers were agentified; 593 of 599 tools passed validation; accuracy 91.2% vs 80.3-86.3% for a coding assistant with the repository; 100% of out-of-scope queries were rejected.
An LLM-assisted workflow had 44.4% sensitivity in its first refinement season, reaching 100% in subsequent seasons after prompt optimisation.

Respiratory conditions affect roughly 20-70% of elite athletes depending on the sport; inhaled corticosteroids are the basis of treatment and short-acting beta-2 agonists alone are not adequate control.

Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is the most common chronic condition in elite sport; resting spirometry is often normal, so exercise challenge or eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea testing is recommended, with anti-doping rules considered in treatment.
Air pollution, aeroallergens, cold or dry air and altitude all modify exercise-induced bronchoconstriction risk.
WHO 2021 guideline levels: PM2.5 5 ug/m3 annual and 15 ug/m3 24-hour; PM10 15 and 45 ug/m3; NO2 10 and 25 ug/m3; ozone 60 ug/m3 peak season and 100 ug/m3 8-hour.

Inhaled beta-2 agonists are permitted within limits: salbutamol 1600 ug, formoterol 54 ug, salmeterol 200 ug and vilanterol 25 ug per 24 hours; other routes are prohibited and urinary thresholds apply.
Brazil's air quality standards are set by CONAMA Resolution 506/2024 and tighten in stages; the PI-2 stage applies from 1 January 2025 and remains less strict than the WHO 2021 guideline levels.
